name: Human and Articulated Avatars
text:
# Human and Articulated Avatars

Also called: Animatable Gaussian Avatars, Dynamic 3DGS Avatars

## Overview
This family extends 3D Gaussian [Splatting](#23-splatting.md) to reconstruct and render animatable human and articulated non-human avatars from multi-view or single-view inputs. It solves the problem of dynamic geometry and appearance modeling by maintaining a canonical space representation where Gaussians are deformed via differentiable functions driven by pose parameters (e.g., skeleton joints, expression coefficients) before [rasterization](#15310-rasterization.md). It sets itself apart from static reconstruction methods by enabling real-time novel view synthesis of dynamic subjects through learned deformation fields or skeletal skinning, and from mesh-based methods by leveraging the explicit, differentiable nature of 3D Gaussians for high-fidelity texture and geometry [S1][S2, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family rely on the differentiable [alpha-blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) accumulation of feature vectors or colors during the rasterization step. For a pixel $p$, the rendered vector $\mathbf{V}(p)$ is computed by sorting overlapping Gaussians $\mathcal{O}_p$ front-to-back and applying:

$$
\mathbf{V}(p) = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{O}_p} \mathbf{v}_i \cdot \alpha_i \cdot \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j)
$$

where:
*   $\mathbf{v}_i$ is the vector (feature $\mathbf{f}_i$ or color $\mathbf{c}_i$) of the $i$-th Gaussian.
*   $\alpha_i$ is the opacity of the $i$-th Gaussian.
*   $\prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j)$ is the transmittance from all preceding Gaussians $j < i$.
*   If $\mathcal{O}_p$ is empty, $\mathbf{V}(p) = \mathbf{0}$.

For structural extensions, all methods share a canonical space representation where 3D Gaussians are initialized in a reference pose (e.g., T-pose or neutral expression). Deformation is achieved by mapping these canonical Gaussians to a target pose defined by parameters (e.g., skeleton joints, expression coefficients). The rendering pipeline remains differentiable, allowing optimization of Gaussian attributes and deformation parameters via photometric loss.

The deformation function $D(\cdot)$ maps a canonical Gaussian $i$ with position $\mathbf{p}_i^{canonical}$ to a target position $\mathbf{p}_i^{target}$ based on pose parameters $\theta$:
$$
\mathbf{p}_i^{target} = D(\mathbf{p}_i^{canonical}, \theta)
$$
The rotation and scale of the Gaussian may also be transformed by the deformation function to maintain physical consistency [G].

## Subtopics

### [GaussianHead](8051-gaussianhead.md)
[GaussianHead](#8051-gaussianhead.md) is a method for animatable head reconstruction that uses a tri-plane representation and motion fields to simulate geometrically changing heads in continuous movements. It is designed to render rich textures, including skin and hair. It differs from siblings like [GART](#8093-gart.md) and [D3GA](#8094-d3ga.md) by explicitly leveraging tri-plane features for deformation rather than relying solely on skeleton-based or mesh-based deformation priors.

### [GART](8093-gart.md)
GART is a 3D Gaussian Splatting-based approach designed to animate articulated non-human models, such as animals, by extending the [canonical space deformation](#12731-deformation-field-parametrization.md) principles originally developed for human avatars. Unlike sibling methods like [GaussianHead](8051-gaussianhead.md) or [D3GA](8094-d3ga.md) which focus on specific human facial or body parts, GART generalizes the template-guided parameterization to broader articulated skeletons. It solves the problem of realistic, real-time rendering of complex, non-human articulated figures by mapping canonical 3D Gaussians to target poses via a differentiable deformation function.

### [D3GA](8094-d3ga.md)
D3GA is a method for creating animatable human avatars using drivable 3D Gaussians and tetrahedral cages for full-body modeling. It addresses the challenge of reconstructing dynamic humans from multi-view videos by providing promising geometry and appearance modeling. It sets itself apart from siblings like [SplatArmor](#8041-splatarmor.md) and [HuGS](#17707-hugs.md) by utilizing tetrahedral cages as the primary deformation structure for the drivable Gaussians.

#### 3D Gaussian Splatting for Human101
*   Push the speed of high-fidelity dynamic human creation to 100 seconds using a fixed-perspective camera [S1][S2, unofficial].

#### SplattingAvatar / GoMAvatar
*   Embed Gaussians onto a canonical human body mesh [S2, unofficial].
*   Determine the position of a Gaussian by the barycenter and displacement along the normal direction [S2, unofficial].

#### HeadGas
*   Attribute the 3DGS with a base of latent features that are weighted by the expression vector from 3DMMs [S2, unofficial].
*   Allow reconstruction in real-time of animatable heads [S2, unofficial].

#### 3DPSHR
*   Combine hand geometry priors (MANO) with 3DGS [S2, unofficial].
*   Provide the first real-time hand reconstruction [S2, unofficial].

#### MonoGaussianAvatar
*   Apply 3DGS to dynamic head reconstruction using canonical space modeling and deformation prediction [S2, unofficial].

#### MANUS
*   Explore the [interaction](#41-interaction.md) between hands and objects using 3DGS [S2, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of animatable avatars using 3D Gaussian Splatting emerged as an extension of static reconstruction methods to handle dynamic subjects. Early works like GaussianAvatar incorporated optimizable tensors with dynamic appearance networks to capture dynamics [S1]. Human101 further optimized the training speed for high-fidelity dynamic human creation, achieving 100 seconds using a fixed-perspective camera [S1][S2, unofficial]. Subsequent methods like [SplattingAvatar](#9556-splattingavatar.md) and [GoMAvatar](#6156-gomavatar.md) embedded Gaussians onto canonical human body meshes, determining positions via barycentric coordinates and normal displacements [S1][S2, unofficial]. For head modeling, MonoGaussianAvatar applied canonical space modeling and deformation prediction [S2, unofficial], while GaussianHead introduced tri-plane representations and motion fields for continuous movement simulation [S2, unofficial]. [HeadGas](#17293-headgas.md) utilized latent features weighted by 3DMM expression vectors for real-time animatable heads [S2, unofficial]. Extensions to other body parts include 3DPSHR for real-time hand reconstruction using MANO priors [S2, unofficial] and MANUS for hand-object interaction [S2, unofficial]. GART extended these principles to non-human articulated models like animals [S1][S2, unofficial], and D3GA introduced tetrahedral cages for full-body human modeling [S1].
